nameStory: The harvestfish gets its name from the timing of its peak abundance, which traditionally coincided with autumn harvest season along the Atlantic coast. Fishermen would find these silvery, coin-shaped fish in their nets just as farmers were bringing in their crops, making it a true 'harvest' from the sea.
description: The harvestfish is a deep-bodied, almost circular fish that looks like someone took a regular fish and compressed it into a silvery disk. These subtropical visitors typically grow to about 8 inches long and have a distinctly round profile with curved fins that flow smoothly around their body. They're greenish-silver on top with bright silver sides that sometimes show a yellowish tint, especially on the belly.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely deep and circular body that feels compressed from side to side, like a silver dollar with fins - much rounder than most fish you'll encounter

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Greenish-silver back transitions to bright silver sides and belly, often with a warm yellow tinge that catches the light like polished metal

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: All fins are curved and flow smoothly around the circular body outline, sometimes appearing slightly dusky or yellowish at the edges

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small mouth positioned at the rounded, blunt nose - noticeably tiny compared to the fish's deep body

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Usually reaches about 8 inches in length, though the deep body makes them appear larger and more substantial than their length suggests

habitat: Harvestfish are extremely rare visitors to New England waters, preferring the warmer subtropical waters from the Chesapeake Bay southward. When they do appear in New England, it's typically in deeper coastal waters during warmer months, possibly following warm water currents northward.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters during spring as they prefer warmer subtropical regions to the south.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter a harvestfish in New England waters if warm currents bring them north, though sightings remain extremely uncommon.
seasonality.fall: Occasional stragglers might still be present in early fall before retreating to warmer southern waters.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having returned to their preferred subtropical range.

funFact: Harvestfish are sometimes called 'star butter fish' because their circular, flattened shape and silvery color make them look like metallic stars when viewed from above - and their flesh is so buttery and tender that they practically melt in your mouth!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its close relative, the butterfish, but harvestfish are much more circular and deep-bodied - think of a silver dollar versus a flattened oval. Remember: harvestfish are 'harvest moon round' while butterfish are more football-shaped.
contextualKnowledge: Harvestfish are sometimes called simply 'butterfish' in local markets, which can cause confusion with the true butterfish that's more common in New England. Both belong to the butterfish family, but they're different species with the harvestfish being much rounder and more southern in range.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the butterfish, harvestfish are much more circular and deep-bodied rather than oval-shaped. While butterfish are common in New England waters, harvestfish are rare subtropical visitors that prefer much warmer waters. The harvestfish's extreme roundness makes it look almost like a different type of fish entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Butterfish can be distinguished from their close relative the harvestfish by their more northern range and slightly different fin proportions.
